name: Sliding genioplasty

lead: Sliding genioplasty reshapes the chin by moving the bone itself. The surgeon cuts the lower part of the chin bone and slides it forward, backward, vertically or sideways, which changes chin projection and width for a stronger, more balanced profile.

Unlike an implant, it uses your own bone, fixed in the new position with plates and screws. It is used for cosmetic chin reshaping, facial feminization and as part of face-contouring and jaw surgery. Evidence consists mostly of case series and reviews, with few comparative trials.

paras: People usually have it done as a planned operation, sometimes alone and sometimes together with other jaw procedures. The result becomes visible as swelling settles. On forums it is discussed as a hardmaxxing option, often compared with chin implants.
Reported problems include swelling, temporary lip and chin numbness, infection, displacement of the bone segment and, more rarely, nerve damage. It does not correct the bite.

angle.text: A stronger, better-balanced chin and profile. The chin bone is cut and moved forward, back or sideways, changing projection or width in a way you can see once healing is done. Evidence is mostly case series with few comparative trials.

lead: Sliding genioplasty is a chin surgery in which a surgeon cuts the lower part of the chin bone and moves it forward, backward, upward, downward or sideways, then fixes it in place with plates and screws [1][2]. Because the surgeon repositions the patient's own bone rather than adding an implant, the result can alter projection, height and width of the chin in a single operation [2][3].

People use it to change facial balance: a small or receding chin can be brought forward so the profile reads as stronger, a long chin can be shortened, a wide or square chin can be narrowed, and a chin can be reshaped to look more feminine or more masculine [1][2][4][5]. It is often combined with rhinoplasty, jaw surgery or face-contouring procedures so that the nose, chin and jaw are planned together [1][6][7].

Published research consists mostly of case series, comparative cohorts and reviews. They describe how far surgeons typically move the bone, how the soft tissue follows, and how often nerve changes or other complications occur [8][7][9][10]. On looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a hardmaxxing option and is regularly compared with chin implants and fillers [11][12][13].

sections.h: What it does and how people use it
paras: The chin is the most prominent element of the lower third of the face in both front and side views, and surgeons plan chin procedures alongside the nose, lips, jaw and neck [14]. A sliding genioplasty is chosen when the patient wants a change in the chin's projection, vertical length or width that goes beyond what an implant or filler can provide [2][6].

Documented uses include advancing a retruded chin, shortening a vertically long chin, centering an off-center chin, creating a narrower, rounder chin for facial feminization, and contouring a square jaw on a short face in East Asian patients [2][4][15][5][3]. Surgeons also use it alongside orthognathic surgery for bite correction, and genioglossus advancement and sliding genioplasty appear in the sleep-apnea surgery literature as ways to open the airway [16].

Wikipedia describes cutting a horseshoe-shaped piece from the lower border of the jaw and repositioning it, held with a titanium step plate and screws; another approach used 26 or 27 gauge wire with the jaws wired together for about three to four weeks [1]. The cut is generally made through the mouth, so there is no external scar [1].

Variants described in the feminization literature include a 1-piece genioplasty that reduces and rounds the chin, a 2-piece genioplasty that changes projection while keeping the shape, and a 3-piece genioplasty that also narrows the chin to give a more V-shaped lower face; protecting the mental nerve and resuspending the mentalis muscle are described as essential [5]. A 3D approach lets the surgeon modify size, form, height and position in all dimensions [3].

The T-osteotomy, or mini V-line, attributed to Korean surgeons, removes an inverted trapezoid of bone so the chin is narrowed and lengthened by a few millimeters, and is fixed with pre-bent titanium plates [1].

Planners use clinical examination, photographs and imaging. A systematic review looked for soft-to-hard tissue ratios, meaning how much the skin profile moves per millimeter of bone movement, to help surgeons plan the size of a sliding genioplasty, bone recontouring or implant augmentation [9]. Cone-beam CT and virtual surgical planning with computer-made guides are described in recent trials and reviews [3][17].

A ten-year series of 474 orthognathic patients reported 155 who had a sliding genioplasty as part of treatment and 37 who had it alone; among the isolated cases, mean advancement was 4.5 mm (range 2 to 7 mm) and mean vertical change was 3.9 mm [7]. Forum users mention surgeons quoting typical advancements of 6 to 7 mm, though that figure comes from a poster's account, not a published series [18].

Chin implants (silicone, porous polyethylene, ePTFE and others) are placed through the mouth or under the chin and sit on the bone surface, while fillers add volume non-surgically for months to years [1]. A retrospective comparison of 345 chin microgenia cases (135 sliding genioplasty, 60 alloplastic implants, 150 hyaluronic acid) concluded that sliding genioplasty gave a more predictable and stable long-term result at three-year follow-up [6].

A review of options says surgical augmentation has long been considered the gold standard but that fillers now allow shaping in three dimensions with minimal downtime [19]. A 1987 two-center trial reported high patient satisfaction, even among patients unhappy with previous implants, and recommended genioplasty as an alternative to alloplastic augmentation in selected patients [10]. The decision typically depends on how much movement is needed, soft-tissue thickness, patient age and preference [6].

Forum posters compare the two: some describe the genioplasty as using one's own bone with no foreign material, while others describe the downsides they have heard of, such as limits on how far the segment can move [11][13].

Wikipedia advises keeping chewing to a minimum right after surgery and eating soft foods for a period [1]. The 1987 trial found average operating time of 43 minutes under local anesthesia in 39 patients and described pain as mild [10]. Patients in forum threads post one-month and later photos and discuss swelling that can look uneven early on; one poster said a surgeon told him the asymmetry would settle as swelling resolved, while a second surgeon pointed to pre-existing asymmetry that more projection made more visible [20].

Reported effects include swelling, hematoma, and temporary lip weakness or numbness; less common are infection, displacement and nerve damage [1]. Mental nerve numbness is the best-studied complication: a 1996 study compared 50 consecutive procedures planned with at least 6 mm between the cut and the nerve canal against 50 earlier ones, and found no permanent nerve injuries in the prospective group versus three in the earlier group [8]. The ten-year series found some degree of mental-nerve paresthesia in almost all patients, usually transient and lasting a few weeks [7]. The 1987 trial reported a 20 percent overall complication rate in 39 patients, including two wound infections and one mental nerve injury [10].

Resuspension of the mentalis muscle is described as important to avoid chin ptosis (a sagging soft tissue chin), and a forum surgeon quoted by a poster warned that moving the chin back can leave extra soft tissue [5][21]. As with any surgery, anesthesia and surgeon experience matter; Wikipedia notes that surgeon experience can reduce complication risk [1].

A systematic review examined soft-to-hard tissue ratios across chin procedures including sliding genioplasty [9]. A ten-year surgeon series described sliding osteotomy for aesthetic balance in 37 isolated cases and 155 combined with jaw surgery [7]. The 345-case comparison favored sliding genioplasty for predictability and stability over implants and fillers at three years [6]. A 1987 prospective two-center trial of 39 patients examined outpatient local-anesthesia genioplasty [10].

A randomized trial in 48 patients undergoing reductive genioplasty compared a piezotome (ultrasonic cutting) technique with traditional instruments and reported less postoperative morbidity and higher long-term satisfaction with the piezotome [22]. A 2024 randomized trial in 33 patients with deficient chins compared autogenous fat, onlay PEEK and sliding genioplasty using CBCT, and reported higher soft-tissue relapse in the fat group at six months, no significant difference between PEEK and genioplasty, and rising satisfaction in all groups [17]; a related registration (NCT03747822) lists 12 patients [23].

Feminization reviews describe the techniques and outcomes of 1-, 2- and 3-piece genioplasty [2][5][3], and a study of popular YouTube videos found most contained poor information content, with individuals' patient-journey videos drawing the most views [24]. Wikipedia notes the underlying literature is mainly case series and reviews [1].

On looksmax.org, genioplasty threads fall into several types: pre-surgery questions about whether it will widen or advance a chin or substitute for bimaxillary surgery [18][12]; implant-versus-genio comparisons [11][13]; cost questions [25]; and post-surgery photo threads that ask for opinions on symmetry [20]. Posters speak of it as a way to 'ascend' or raise a PSL score, and one thread asks whether a genioplasty alone could produce a particular rating [26].

Community advice is mixed, with some replies telling the original poster to proceed and others saying a bite problem would need jaw surgery instead [12]. Posters also discuss combining it with rhinoplasty and jaw implants, and moving the chin back during bimax surgery [20][21].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sliding genioplasty is discussed as a way to improve profile or chin width, often weighed against implants or jaw surgery [11][18][13].

claims.claim: Sliding genioplasty can widen a narrow chin
Genioplasty can compensate for a poor bite or weak jaw
Using your own bone is more reliable than an implant
Early asymmetry after surgery is usually swelling
A genioplasty alone can move someone up a PSL tier
Genioplasty can move a chin back as well as forward
Nerve numbness is a rare and temporary risk

timeline.event: Aufricht's report on combined nose and chin surgery is among the early works cited by Wikipedia's chin article [1].
A prospective two-center trial of 39 patients tests sliding genioplasty as an outpatient local-anesthesia procedure [10].
A prospective study of 50 genioplasties reports no permanent mental nerve injuries when at least 6 mm was kept from the nerve canal [8].
A ten-year series reports isolated and combined sliding genioplasties for aesthetic balance [7].
A historical review notes that surgical approaches to chin deformities began in the second half of the twentieth century, with silicone prostheses and sliding genioplasty [14].
A technique for narrowing and sliding genioplasty with outer-cortex ostectomy is published for square jaws in East Asian patients [4].
A systematic review of soft-to-hard tissue ratios in chin procedures and a 345-case comparison with implants and fillers are published [6][9].
A randomized trial compares piezotome and traditional genioplasty [22].
Reviews describe osteotomy-based chin feminization; a trial of fat or PEEK versus genioplasty is registered [2][23].
A review describes 3D sliding genioplasty for facial feminization [3].
A randomized trial compares fat, PEEK and sliding genioplasty for deficient chins [17].
